patient.chief_complaint: Recurrent episodes of sudden intense fear, palpitations, and a feeling of unreality, diagnosed as panic attacks but worsening despite treatment
patient.history_present_illness:
Ms. Delgado is a 29-year-old right-handed elementary school teacher who presents for inpatient evaluation of recurrent paroxysmal episodes that have been diagnosed as panic attacks over the past two years but have been escalating in frequency and are now occurring daily despite adequate treatment with sertraline and as-needed lorazepam. She describes the episodes as beginning with a sudden, overwhelming surge of fear that she describes as unlike normal anxiety, as though something terrible is about to happen but she cannot identify what. This is accompanied by a peculiar sensation she struggles to articulate, describing it variously as her stomach flipping, a wave of warmth rising from her abdomen to her chest, and occasionally a strange smell that she says is like burning rubber that nobody else around her can detect. During some episodes she experiences a profound feeling of depersonalization, as though the world around her has become unfamiliar and dreamlike.

The episodes typically last between 30 seconds and two minutes. Her boyfriend has witnessed several and reports that during the more intense ones, she stops speaking mid-sentence, stares vacantly, and appears to chew or smack her lips. She has no memory of these observed behaviors and initially denied they occurred until he recorded one on his phone. Following the more prolonged episodes she feels confused and exhausted for 10 to 20 minutes. She has never had a convulsive episode or lost consciousness in a dramatic fashion.

She was evaluated by her primary care physician who increased her sertraline from 50 mg to 100 mg and referred her to psychiatry. Her psychiatrist diagnosed refractory panic disorder and added lorazepam. A cardiologist evaluated her palpitations and attributed them to her known mitral valve prolapse and anxiety, obtaining a normal Holter monitor. Over the past three months, the episodes have increased from weekly to near-daily, occurring unpredictably during work, rest, and even during sleep on at least two occasions where her boyfriend observed her sitting up in bed, staring, and making repetitive hand movements. She has taken medical leave from teaching because an episode occurred in front of her students. She is now referred to neurology for further evaluation after her psychiatrist questioned whether these could be epileptic in nature.

results.title: Ictal fear is a common semiology in temporal lobe epilepsy and is frequently misdiagnosed as panic disorder
results.summary: Ictal fear occurs in 10-20% of temporal lobe epilepsy patients and is the most common aura type in right temporal lobe seizures. The mean diagnostic delay when ictal fear is the predominant symptom is 7.4 years due to misdiagnosis as panic disorder.

results.title: Differentiating panic attacks from temporal lobe seizures
results.summary: Key distinguishing features include: seizure episodes are briefer (30-120 seconds vs 10-30 minutes for panic), stereotyped, associated with altered awareness, have post-ictal confusion, may occur from sleep, and often include olfactory or gustatory hallucinations. Panic attacks rarely have olfactory hallucinations and patients retain awareness.

results.title: MRI-negative focal epilepsy: prevalence, outcomes, and the role of advanced imaging
results.summary: Approximately 20-30% of focal epilepsy patients have normal standard MRI. 3T epilepsy protocol MRI, FDG-PET, and post-processing techniques can identify subtle lesions (especially focal cortical dysplasia) in up to 30% of previously MRI-negative cases.

output.summary: Ictal fear occurs in 10-20% of temporal lobe epilepsy patients and is most common in right temporal lobe seizures, with a mean diagnostic delay of approximately 7 years due to misdiagnosis as panic disorder. Key distinguishing features include: episodes lasting under 2 minutes, stereotyped semiology, occurrence from sleep, automatisms with impaired awareness, post-ictal confusion, and olfactory hallucinations. Routine EEG sensitivity for focal epilepsy is 29-55%; prolonged video-EEG monitoring significantly increases diagnostic yield. Approximately 20-30% of focal epilepsy patients are MRI-negative on standard imaging; 3T epilepsy protocol MRI and FDG-PET can identify subtle lesions in up to 30% of these cases.

optimal_actions.action: Obtain detailed seizure history including semiology, aura, automatisms, duration, frequency, witness accounts, and post-ictal features.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Stereotyped focal impaired-awareness events with temporal-lobe aura and post-ictal confusion.
Interictal exam typically normal; subtle memory deficit may be present.

optimal_actions.action: Order EEG (long-term video-EEG monitoring) to identify interictal epileptiform discharges and capture habitual events.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Interictal sharps/spikes and/or focal slowing in the anterior temporal region; ictal correlate confirms diagnosis.

optimal_actions.action: Order MRI brain with dedicated epilepsy protocol (thin-cut coronal T1/FLAIR/T2/DWI through the hippocampi).
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Hippocampal sclerosis, low-grade tumor (DNET, ganglioglioma), cavernoma, or focal cortical dysplasia; rule out alternative structural causes.

optimal_actions.action: Obtain CBC, comprehensive metabolic panel, prolactin (if drawn within 10–20 min of event), and AED levels if on therapy.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Exclude metabolic provocation (hypoglycemia, hyponatremia, uremia); baseline organ function for AED selection; AED level for adherence and dosing.

useless_tools.rationale: No clinical features of CNS infection, encephalitis, or immunocompromise; CSF analysis is not indicated for routine focal epilepsy workup and exposes the patient to procedural risk and cost.
No syncope-versus-seizure question and no structural-heart concern; echocardiogram contributes nothing to epilepsy workup.
Ambulatory cardiac monitoring is reserved for syncope-versus-seizure differentiation; not indicated when semiology is clearly epileptic.
Non-contrast head CT is inferior to MRI for detecting epileptogenic substrates (hippocampal sclerosis, FCD, low-grade tumor) and adds ionizing radiation without diagnostic yield.

sequence_constraints.reason: Structural cause influences AED choice (e.g., low-grade tumor → consider AEDs with CYP-neutral profile; hippocampal sclerosis → multiple equally appropriate options). MRI should inform drug selection.

critical_actions: Recognize stereotyped ictal fear with behavioral arrest, automatisms, and post-ictal confusion as focal impaired-awareness seizures rather than panic.
Apply ILAE drug-resistance criteria (failure of ≥2 appropriately chosen and tolerated AEDs) and refer to a comprehensive epilepsy center.
Capture habitual events with long-term video-EEG to confirm onset zone.
Obtain 3T MRI with dedicated epilepsy protocol; if MRI is non-localizing, proceed to FDG-PET for metabolic localization.
Engage a multidisciplinary epilepsy surgery team for presurgical evaluation.
contraindicated_actions: Do not escalate anxiolytic therapy or label as treatment-resistant panic without epilepsy workup.
Do not perform lumbar puncture without specific concern for encephalitis.
Do not start a third AED at full dose before reviewing adherence, AED levels, and the diagnostic certainty.
key_reasoning_points: Drug-resistant epilepsy (Kwan 2010 criteria) mandates referral to a comprehensive epilepsy center.
Ictal fear can be a temporal-lobe semiology and is the most common cause of 'medically refractory panic.'
Long-term video-EEG is required to confirm electrographic onset and lateralization.
MRI-negative TLE benefits from FDG-PET, which shows focal hypometabolism ipsilateral to the seizure focus in ~70% of cases.
Neuropsychological lateralization informs surgical risk for memory decline.
